summary: A first-person account of a community gathering on September 15, 2023 to open a time capsule buried in autumn 1973 in the town square. Instead of the usual newspapers, it held blueprints and scale models of local architecture, including the library, train station, Hasselback farmhouse and Donovan Family Theatre. The author reflects on how the town has changed and how these artifacts connect generations.
one_line: A writer recounts the 2023 opening of a 1973 town time capsule filled with architectural blueprints and models, reflecting on change and continuity.
key_facts: The time capsule was unearthed on September 15, 2023 at the old town square, after being buried half a century earlier in autumn 1973.
Instead of mementos or old newspapers, the capsule contained blueprints and scale models of local architecture.
The original blueprints of the Victorian local library were signed by architect Jonathan McDowell on November 12, 1973.
McDowell's library design combined ornate gables with subtle Art Nouveau curves, with hand-carved wooden bannisters and secret reading nooks that are no longer part of the modernized building.
A scale model of the old train station was crafted by local artisan Eleanor Whitfield and her son Jeremy on September 22, 1973, complete with wooden benches and a small flower shop.
The old train station has since been replaced by a hub of gleaming metal and glass.
A blueprint dated October 2, 1973 showed the Hasselback family homestead; the farmlands and silos are now replaced by sleek condominiums and eco-friendly buildings with rooftop gardens.
Cecilia Donovan inked the blueprints of the Donovan Family Theatre on September 30, 1973, with sketches of the stage design and velvet-curtained balconies.
The author grew up with the Donovan Family Theatre as a sanctuary, the place of a first standing ovation and first heartbreak.
The author sees the blueprints and models as a bridge between generations and a measure of social, technological and aesthetic evolution.
